name: WHAMR!
ability_definition: The ability to focus on a single source of sound in the presence of other distracting sounds.

task_realism.reasoning: The core challenge is pulling a voice out of competing talkers, real recorded ambient noise (cafés, restaurants) and reverberation, which is the acoustic core of auditory attention. However, the speech is read WSJ news text, the mixtures are artificially summed with simulated room impulse responses, and there are exactly two speakers. Real workplace settings such as call centers, dispatch, noisy shop floors and meetings involve spontaneous speech, variable numbers of talkers and real acoustics.

evaluation_conditions.reasoning: Evaluation is offline on pre-segmented utterances with unlimited compute. Leading systems even use repeated inference passes and dataset-specific fine-tuning. There is no real-time or streaming constraint, no stakes and no distribution shift. The test set closely matches the training distribution in simulation pipeline and speaker pool, unlike the unpredictable conditions of real work.

construct_coverage.reasoning: It measures only low-level signal separation of all sources. It does not test selectively attending to a cued or relevant target, tracking a target as it switches or moves, or handling more than two talkers or non-speech targets. It also does not test whether the attended content is actually understood. These are key parts of human auditory attention in work settings.

format_match.reasoning: The input is a realistic artifact, a single-channel noisy reverberant audio waveform. The output is separated waveforms scored by a reference-based SI-SNRi metric. That is an engineering proxy rather than a workplace output such as a transcript, a correctly followed instruction or a response to the target speaker.

transferability_reasoning: WHAMR! captures the acoustic essence of attending to one voice amid competing talkers, noise and reverberation, so it is more relevant than clean WSJ0-2mix. Its transfer is limited by simulated two-speaker read-speech mixtures, offline evaluation that permits heavy compute, and an all-source separation objective scored by SI-SNRi rather than cued target selection or comprehension. Gains in dB therefore say only moderately much about real workplace listening in noisy environments.

2024.metric: SI-SNRi (scale-invariant signal-to-noise ratio improvement), dB, higher is better
2024.human_reference: General adult workforce with normal hearing: people who routinely follow one talker in noisy, reverberant settings such as cafes, restaurants and open offices.

2025.metric: SI-SNRi, dB (higher is better); SDRi 18.2 dB
2025.human_reference: General adult listeners with normal hearing: the typical person who must follow one talker amid competing speech, noise and room reverberation at work. Examples are open offices, meetings and call centres. They listen monaurally, as on a single-channel recording or phone line.
